en: The Sūtra on Maitreya’s Descent into the World, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
He was together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.
At that time, Ānanda bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The Tathāgata’s profound discernment perceives all things; he clearly understands all three periods of time—future, past, and present.”
He fully knows the surnames, given names, and titles of all past Buddhas, as well as the number of their disciples, bodhisattvas, and attendants;
he likewise observes all eons—whether a single eon, a hundred eons, or incalculable eons—in this same manner;
and he is able to distinguish the surnames and names of kings, ministers, and the common people.
Now, the various conditions of the realm in the present are clearly understood.

As for the distant future when Maitreya appears as a Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha—desiring to hear of those transformations, his disciples and followers, and how long the Buddha-field will remain prosperous and joyful.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Return to your seat and listen as I describe the abundance and joy of Maitreya’s land upon his appearance, as well as the number of his disciples."
"Reflect upon this well and hold it in your heart.
At that time, Ānanda received the instruction from the Buddha and immediately returned to his seat.
Then, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:

"In the distant future, within this realm, there shall be a city named Ketumatī, twelve yojanas from east to west and seven yojanas from south to north. Its lands shall be fertile and prosperous, its population vast and flourishing, with streets and lanes laid out in orderly rows."
At that time, there was a dragon king in the city named Water-Light (Jala-prabha), who rained down fragrant moisture by night and made the days clear and mild.

At that time, in the city of Ketumatī, there was a rākṣasa named Leaf-Flower (Patra-puṣpa) who acted in accordance with the Dharma and did not contravene the true teaching; every time after the people had fallen asleep, he would remove all filth and impurities;
he constantly sprinkled the ground with fragrant liquid, making it exceedingly pure and sweet-smelling.

“Ānanda, you should know that at that time, throughout the ten directions of Jambudvīpa for thousands of millions of yojanas, all mountains, rivers, and rocky cliffs will naturally vanish, and the waters of the four great oceans will each decrease by ten thousand [yojanas].”
At that time, Jambudvīpa was exceedingly level and as clear and bright as a mirror.
Throughout the entire land of Jambudvīpa, grain was abundant and cheap; the population was flourishing, and there were many precious treasures.
The various villages were situated close together, with the crowing of their roosters reaching one another.
At that time, trees bearing inferior flowers and fruits withered away, and all impurities likewise vanished;
instead, other trees bearing sweet and delicious fruits, as well as those with exquisite fragrances, sprang up from the earth.

"At that time, the seasonal climate was harmonious and the four seasons followed their proper order; within the bodies of human beings, there were no afflictions of the one hundred and eight [defilements]:
namely, greed, anger, and delusion, nor was there any lack of earnest diligence."
The minds of people were impartial and even, all sharing a single intention; they greeted one another with joy and addressed each other with kind words.
Their speech was of one kind without any distinction, just like that of the people of Uttarakuru, no different from them.
At that time, the people within Jambudvīpa, both great and small, were all of one mind, without any distinctions between them.
At that time, whenever men and women desired to relieve themselves, the earth would naturally open; once their business was finished, the earth would immediately close back together.
"At that time, within Jambudvīpa, non-glutinous rice grew spontaneously; it was without husks, exceedingly fragrant and delicious, and its consumption caused no affliction or suffering.
Furthermore, gold, silver, precious gems, musāragalva, agate, pearls, and amber were scattered everywhere upon the ground, yet no one took note of them."
At that time, the people took hold of this treasure in their hands and said to one another:
"In the past, because of this treasure, people harmed one another, were imprisoned in jails, and underwent countless sufferings;
now this treasure is treated no differently than common tiles and stones, with no one to guard it."
"At that time, a Dharma King appeared, named Śaṅkha.
He ruled and transformed the world through the True Dharma, and the seven treasures were perfected.

As for what are called the seven treasures: the wheel treasure, the elephant treasure, the horse treasure, the jewel treasure, the woman-treasure, the military commander treasure, and the treasury-guardian treasure—these are known as the seven treasures."
He pacifies this Jambudvīpa without using weapons or force, and all naturally submit.
Now, Ānanda, there are four treasuries of jewels:
In the kingdom of Gandhāra, there is the Airāvata treasure-store, containing countless rare and extraordinary objects beyond measure;
second, in the kingdom of Mithilā, there is the Caura great treasury, which also contains many precious jewels;
third, in the great kingdom of Sūrata, there is a great treasure-store, which likewise contains many precious jewels.
In the fourth region, Vārāṇasī, there is a great treasure-store containing immeasurable and incalculable varieties of rare jewels.
These four great treasuries spontaneously appeared, and the guardians of each storehouse came individually to inform the king:
"We pray that Your Majesty will bestow these treasures from the storehouses upon the poor."
At that time, after King Śaṅkha had obtained this treasure, he likewise did not take note of it, for his mind harbored no thought of wealth or jewels.

Then, within Jambudvīpa, garments grew spontaneously upon trees—extremely fine and soft—which people took and wore; they were no different from the garments that grow spontaneously on trees for the people of Uttarakuru.
"At that time, that king had a great minister named Sūvīra, who had been his companion since childhood; the king held him in great affection and respect.
Furthermore, his appearance was handsome: he was neither tall nor short, neither fat nor thin, neither too pale nor too dark, and neither old nor young."

At that time, Suddhodana had a wife named Mahāmāyā, the most exquisite among the daughters of kings, like the consort of Śakra. Her mouth exhaled the fragrance of the *utpala* lotus, and her body emitted the scent of sandalwood;
she was forever free from the eighty-four feminine affectations and possessed no thoughts of illness or distraction.

"At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva, while in the Tuṣita Heaven, observed that his parents were neither too old nor too young; he then descended from the divine realm and was born from the right side of the womb, no different from my own birth today from the right side—Maitreya Bodhisattva shall likewise be so."
The various devas of Tuṣita each proclaimed:
"Maitreya Bodhisattva has already descended to take birth.
At that time, Śuddhodana immediately conferred a name upon his son, calling him Maitreya.
Maitreya Bodhisattva’s body is adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, and his body is the color of gold.
At that time, the human lifespan will be exceedingly long; free from all ailments, all shall live for eighty-four thousand years.
Women shall reach the age of five hundred years before they marry.
At that time, Maitreya, having not remained in the household for long, shall immediately leave the home life to study the Way.
At that time, not far from the city of Ketumatī, there was a tree of the Way named Nāgapuṣpa, one yojana high and five hundred paces wide.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva sat beneath that tree and attained the fruit of the unsurpassed Way.
"At midnight, when Maitreya leaves the household life, he shall attain the Unsurpassed Way on that very night.
At that time, the trichiliocosm will tremble in six ways, and the earth deities will each announce to one another:
'At this moment, Maitreya has become a Buddha.'"
The news spread until it reached the palaces of the Four Heavenly Kings, who heard:
"Maitreya has already attained the Way of the Buddha.

From there, the sound progressively reached the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven; the report was passed along until it reached the Brahma Heaven.
"Maitreya has already attained the Buddha-way.
At that time, there was a Mara King named Mahāsenāpati who ruled and transformed others through the Dharma.
Upon hearing the sound of the Tathāgata’s name, he leaped for joy so intensely that he could not contain himself; for seven days and seven nights, he neither slept nor rested.
At that time, Māra led countless devas and humans of the desire realm to the presence of Maitreya Buddha to pay respectful homage.

The Holy Honored One Maitreya gradually expounded for the devas and humans a subtle and wondrous discourse; that is to say, the discourse on giving, the discourse on morality, and the discourse on rebirth in heaven, [explaining that] the perception of the impurity of desire and the excellence of renunciation are the essentials.

At that time, Maitreya, seeing that the people had already resolved their minds with joy, extensively analyzed and explained the meaning of the Dharma constantly taught by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones—the suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—to all the devas and humans.
At that time, eighty-four thousand devaputras on the seats were cleansed of all defilements and attained the pure Dharma-eye.
Then, the Great General Māra addressed the people of that realm, saying:
"All of you, quickly leave the household life!"
"Why is this so? Maitreya has today already crossed to the other shore, and he shall likewise lead you all to cross to that other shore.

At that time, in the city of Ketumatī, there was an elder named Sudhana. Having heard the command of the Māra King and also having heard the resonance of the Buddha’s voice, he led a multitude of eighty-four thousand people to the place where Maitreya Buddha was. He prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha's feet and sat to one side.

"At that time, Maitreya gradually expounded for them the subtle and profound discourse on the Dharma; that is to say, the discourse on giving, the discourse on morality, and the discourse on rebirth in heaven, [explaining that] the perception of impurity regarding sensual desires and the excellence of the path of renunciation are supreme."

At that time, seeing that the minds of the people had opened and their intentions were resolved, Maitreya extensively analyzed the meaning of the Dharma as it is always taught by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones—namely, suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—for the sake of the people.
At that time, the eighty-four thousand people seated there were cleansed of all defilements and attained the pure Dharma-eye.

Then, Sudhana and the eighty-four thousand others immediately stepped forward before the Buddha, requesting to leave the household life to cultivate the holy life with excellence, until they all achieved the path of Arhatship.
"At that time, in Maitreya’s first assembly, eighty-four thousand people attained arhatship.
At that moment, King Śaṅkha, hearing that Maitreya had already realized the path of Buddhahood, went to where the Buddha was in order to hear the Dharma."

At that time, Maitreya Buddha preached the Dharma for the king—a teaching that was excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end, with its principles profound and far-reaching.

Then, at another time, the great king installed his crown prince as the new king, bestowed precious jewels upon the barber, and gave various treasures to the brahmins. Leading a multitude of eighty-four thousand followers, he went to the Buddha’s dwelling to seek ordination as śramaṇas; they all attained the fruits of the Path and became arhats.

At that time, the great elder Śuddhodana, hearing that Maitreya had already attained the path of Buddhahood, led a multitude of eighty-four thousand brahmins to the Buddha’s dwelling to seek ordination as śramaṇas; they all attained arhatship—except for Śuddhodana alone, who severed the three fetters and was destined to reach the end of suffering.
"At that time, the Buddha’s mother, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, again led a retinue of eighty-four thousand ladies to the place where the Buddha was, seeking to become śramaṇīs.
At that moment, all those women attained arhatship—except for Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī alone, who severed the three fetters and became a srotāpanna."

"At that time, when the Kṣatriya women heard that Maitreya Tathāgata had appeared in the world and attained equal and perfect enlightenment, several tens of millions of them went to the Buddha’s dwelling, prostrated themselves at his feet with their heads and faces touching them, and sat to one side. Each gave rise to the thought of seeking to become a śramaṇa, leaving the household life to study the Way; some attained realization by skipping stages, while others did not attain realization."
"At that time, Ānanda!

Those who did not bypass the stages to attain realization were all people devoted to the Dharma; they were weary of and disgusted with all worldly existence, cultivating the perception of its lack of delight."
"At that time, Maitreya shall preach the teachings of the Three Vehicles just as I do today.
Among his disciples, Mahākāśyapa—who practiced the twelve dhūtas and cultivated pure conduct under past Buddhas—shall assist Maitreya in exhorting and transforming the people."
At that time, Kāśyapa sat cross-legged not far from the Tathāgata, straightening his body and composing his mind, binding his mindfulness before him.
Then the World-Honored One addressed Kāśyapa, saying:
"I am now advanced in years, having reached over eighty."
However, the Tathāgata now has four great śrāvakas who are capable of traveling to convert others; their wisdom is inexhaustible and they are fully endowed with all virtues. Who are these four?
They are the bhikṣu Mahākāśyapa, the bhikṣu Trapusa, the bhikṣu Piṇḍola-bharadvāja, and the bhikṣu Rāhula.
"You four great śrāvakas must not enter parinirvāṇa; you shall only enter parinirvāṇa after my Dharma has completely disappeared.
Mahākāśyapa likewise should not enter parinirvāṇa until Maitreya appears in the world."

The reason for this is that all the disciples transformed by Maitreya were originally disciples of Śākyamuni; it is through my remaining influence that they have been able to exhaust their outflows (*āsrava*).
"In the village of Vitī within the kingdom of Magadha, Mahākāśyapa dwells upon that mountain."

Furthermore, when the Tathāgata Maitreya, surrounded by a multitude of countless thousands of followers, comes to this mountain, the various spirits shall, by the grace of the Buddha, open the gate for him so that he may behold the meditation cave of Kāśyapa.
At that time, Maitreya extended his right hand, pointed toward Kāśyapa, and addressed the multitude:
"In the distant past, there was a disciple of Śākyamuni Buddha named Kāśyapa; he is present here today, foremost among those who practice the dhūta austerities."

At that time, when the people saw this event, they marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence; hundreds of thousands of sentient beings were cleansed of all defilements and attained the pure Dharma-eye.

Furthermore, there were sentient beings who, upon seeing the body of Kāśyapa—this being called the first assembly—nine hundred and sixty million people all attained arhatship; these individuals were all my disciples.
Why is this so? It is entirely due to the fact that they have received my instruction, and it is also due to four causal conditions:
generosity, loving-kindness, benefiting others, and impartial benefit.
"At that time, Ānanda!
Maitreya Tathāgata shall take up the saṃghāṭī robe of Kāśyapa and wear it.
At that moment, Kāśyapa’s body will suddenly disperse like stars."
At that time, Maitreya again took various kinds of flowers and incense to make offerings to Kāśyapa.
Why was this? It is because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess a heart of reverence for the True Dharma.
Maitreya, too, has attained the unsurpassed, true, and correct path through being transformed by the True Dharma received from me.

Ānanda, you should know that at the second assembly of Maitreya Buddha, there will be nine hundred and forty million people who are all arhats; they, too, were disciples of my bequeathed teaching, and their attainment was brought about by their practice of the four kinds of offerings.
"Furthermore, at Maitreya’s third assembly, nine hundred and twenty billion people will all be arhats; they too shall be my disciples of the bequeathed teaching.
At that time, the surnames and names of the bhikṣus will all be called 'Disciples of Maitreya,' just as all the śrāvakas of my own day are called 'Disciples of Śākyamuni.'"
At that time, Maitreya was teaching the Dharma to his disciples: "O bhikṣus!

You should contemplate the perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering in what is pleasant, the perception of non-self in what is conceived as self, the perception of emptiness in reality, the perception of the transformation of form, the perception of lividness, the perception of bloating, the perception of undigested food, the perception of pus and blood, and the perception that all worlds are not worth delighting in."
Why is this so? Monks, you should know that these ten perceptions were all taught to you by the past Śākyamuni Buddha, so that you might exhaust all taints and attain liberation of mind.
If among this assembly there are disciples of Śākyamuni Buddha who, having practiced the holy life (brahmacarya) in the past, have come to my presence;
or those who, having made offerings to the Triple Gem under Śākyamuni Buddha, have come to my presence;
or those who, having cultivated roots of goodness for even the duration of a finger-snap under Śākyamuni Buddha, have arrived here;
Some have come here having practiced the four immeasurable minds under Śākyamuni Buddha;
some have come to my place having received and upheld the five precepts and the Dharma of the three refuges under Śākyamuni Buddha;
and some have come to my place having established divine temples and shrines under Śākyamuni Buddha.
Some have repaired old temples at the site of Śākyamuni Buddha and come to my place;
some have received the eightfold precepts of the fast from Śākyamuni Buddha and come to my place;
and some have made offerings of incense and flowers to Śākyamuni Buddha and have come here.
Or again, some may come to my presence after weeping and shedding tears upon hearing the Dharma there;
or again, some may come to my presence after listening to and receiving the Dharma with single-minded devotion from Śākyamuni Buddha;
or again, some may come to my presence after having perfectly cultivated the holy life (brahmacarya) for as long as their lives lasted.
"Or again, there may be those who come to my presence to copy, read, or recite [this teaching];
or again, there may be those who come to my presence to serve and make offerings.
At that time, Maitreya spoke these verses:
“Having increased the virtues of precepts and learning, and having practiced the tasks of meditation and reflection,
you have well cultivated the holy life and come to my presence.”
Exhorting others to give, they give rise to a joyful mind; practicing the fundamental source of the mind, their thoughts are free from manifold distractions, and all have come to my presence.
Some have given rise to a mind of equanimity, serving and honoring all Buddhas.
Those who offered rice and sweets to the assembly of noble ones have all come to my presence.
Those who recited the precepts and the sūtras, who skillfully practiced and explained them to others,
and who zealously applied themselves to the foundations of the Dharma, have now come to my presence.
The Śākyas are skilled in transformation; having made offerings to the various śarīras and performed the service of Dharma-offerings, they have now come to my presence.
If there are those who transcribe the sutras and proclaim them upon white silk, [they shall likewise attain this].
Those who have made offerings to the sutras all come to my place;
those who offer silk, brocade, and various goods to divine shrines,
and who call themselves "Namo Buddha," all come to my place.
Making offerings to the Buddhas of the present and those of the past,
their meditative concentration is perfectly equanimous, without increase or decrease.
Therefore, within the Buddha-dharma, one should serve the noble Saṃgha.
"Devoting one's mind exclusively to the Three Jewels, one will surely reach the state of non-action.
"Ānanda, you should know that the Tathāgata Maitreya will speak these verses amidst that assembly."
At that time, among that assembly, the devas and human beings who contemplated these ten perceptions—eleven koṭis of people were cleansed of all defilements and attained the pure Dharma-eye.
During the thousand-year reign of Tathāgata Maitreya, the community of monks shall be free from all blemish.
At that time, they shall always take a single verse as their precept:
"Let the mouth and mind commit no evil, And let the body likewise refrain from transgression."
"When these three practices are eliminated, one will swiftly escape the barrier of birth and death.
"After more than a thousand years have passed, there shall be those who violate the precepts; consequently, the precepts shall be established once again."
“The Tathāgata Maitreya shall have a lifespan of eighty-four thousand years.
After his parinirvāṇa, his bequeathed Dharma shall remain for eighty-four thousand years.
This is because, at that time, all sentient beings will possess sharp faculties.”

“If there are sons of good family or daughters of good family who wish to see Maitreya Buddha, as well as the assembly of Śrāvakas at his three assemblies, the city of Ketumatī, and King Śaṅkha along with the four great treasuries of precious jewels; who wish to eat naturally grown non-glutinous rice and wear naturally produced garments; and who wish that upon the dissolution of the body and the end of life they be reborn in the heavens—those sons and daughters of good family should apply themselves with diligent vigor and never give rise to indolence.
They should also serve and honor the Dharma masters, making offerings of various kinds such as famous flowers and powdered incense, ensuring that no opportunity for practice is lost.”
"In this way, Ānanda,
you should train yourself.
At that time, Ānanda and the entire great assembly, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

Regarding the *Buddhabhāṣita-maitreya-sūtra* (The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on Maitreya’s Descent): according to the *Kaiyuan lu*, it was translated but no manuscript exists among the extant texts. Among those works, there is the *Maitreya-buddhatva-sūtra* translated by Dharmarakṣa, also known as the *Maitreya-āgamiṣyanirvāṇa-sūtra*.
At first glance, it may seem that this sutra was lost and then recovered; however, in reality, this is not the case.
Why is this so? Under the title of Kumārajīva’s translation of the *Maitreya-buddhābhisaṃbodhi-sūtra*, there is a note which states:

"It is a different recension from the *Xiasheng jing* (Sūtra on the Descent) and shares the same original text as Dharmarakṣa’s translation of the *Mile chengfo jing* (Sūtra on Maitreya Attaining Buddhahood).

Since one of these two translations is missing [in certain collections], it is clear that it is the lost original of that [latter work], rather than being one of the three lost versions among the six translations of this *Xiasheng jing*."
Furthermore, according to the "Postscript to the Re-edited *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*" by Zhìyuán of Gushan:
"The ancient masters who divided the sūtra all used the number of sheets as their standard; one sheet contains twenty-five lines, and each line contains seventeen characters."
Now, upon examining the lost catalog of the *Maitreya Sūtra*, the sub-commentary states:

"Seventeen sheets," which calculates to seven thousand two hundred and twenty-two characters. This present sūtra contains only three thousand one hundred and seventy-six characters, which is not even half of that number; how could this possibly be that sūtra?
Thus, it is fortunate that this scripture is not found in the Danzang (Dunhuang Canon).

However, the text of this scripture bears a strong resemblance to those of the Han and Jin dynasties; furthermore, the scriptural commentary contains the phrase "Han yun" (the Han say). Consequently, I fear this may be the first of the three lost versions.
The catalog states that it was merely appended to the Western Jin collection, and that the Song canon subsequently recovered it and included it therein; thus, its inclusion there is justified.
Yet, neither of the two catalogs lists a *Xiasheng jing* (Sūtra of the Descent) as a translation by Dharmarakṣa. Why, then, is it now said to be a translation by Dharmarakṣa?
I prostrate myself and await the arrival of the worthy and wise.
